title: Wildlife Ecology & Management
short: The science and professional management of free-ranging wild animals: estimating populations, understanding movement and habitat, and deciding how agencies and organizations should act.
bigPicture: Wildlife ecology and management applies ecological science to free-ranging animal populations and the habitats and human systems that shape them. It combines population estimation, movement and habitat analysis, field techniques, law, policy, and public decision-making. The work is organized around practical questions: whether a population is secure, what is causing change, which action is feasible, and how its results will be measured.

distinction.title: Wildlife Ecology & Management and Ecology
distinction.summary: The fields share population biology, field sampling, statistics, and spatial analysis. What they centre on, and what they produce, are different.

items.label: Wildlife Ecology & Management
items.description: Centers on free-ranging wild animals, their populations, and the habitats and people affecting them. Typical products include population estimates, species and habitat plans, harvest or protection recommendations, permits, and evaluated management actions.

items.label: Ecology
items.description: Examines relationships across living systems. A project might center on microbes, plants, animals, species interactions, nutrient cycles, disturbance, or ecosystem function. Typical products include scientific explanations, models, monitoring results, and environmental assessments.

terms.definition: Marking a sample of animals, then using how many marked animals turn up later to estimate total population size.

focus.title: Focal wildlife populations
focus.description: Estimating abundance, survival, reproduction, distribution, and trend for particular wild species using surveys, marking, and statistical estimation.

focus.title: Habitat and land management
focus.description: Evaluating what habitat a species needs and managing land to provide it, including restoration, disturbance regimes, and working with landowners.
focus.source: Michigan State: Wildlife Ecology and Management B.S.

focus.title: Species and program management
focus.description: Setting and implementing management for game, nongame, endangered, and invasive species, usually inside an agency framework with legal mandates.
focus.source: Michigan State: Wildlife Ecology and Management B.S.

focus.title: Human dimensions
focus.description: Wildlife management is as much about people as animals: stakeholders, conflict, regulation, and public expectation are part of the professional core, not an add-on.
focus.source: Michigan State: Wildlife Ecology and Management B.S.

questions.question: How many are there, and is the number changing?
questions.approach: Through survey designs that account for animals you fail to detect — mark-recapture, distance sampling, occupancy modeling — since raw counts almost always undercount.

questions.question: What habitat does this population need, and is it available?
questions.approach: By relating animal locations to measured habitat features, often with tracking data and remote sensing, then mapping where suitable habitat actually exists.

questions.question: Where do these animals go, and when?
questions.approach: By fitting tracking devices and analyzing movement paths for migration routes, home ranges, corridors, and barriers.

questions.question: What management action would change the outcome, and at what cost?
questions.approach: By modeling alternative scenarios against population objectives and comparing expected results to budget and staff realities.

questions.question: Is this harvest or take level sustainable?
questions.approach: By combining population estimates with survival and reproduction data in a population model, then setting limits with a margin for uncertainty.

questions.question: How do people's interests and behavior shape what is possible?
questions.approach: Through stakeholder surveys, public meetings, and human dimensions research, treating social data with the same rigor as biological data.

responsibilities: Plan and conduct field surveys, capture, and monitoring programs.
Analyze population and habitat data and produce estimates with uncertainty.
Write management plans, technical reports, and permit documentation.
Coordinate with landowners, agencies, and the public.
knowledgeSkills: Field survey, capture, and handling techniques
Statistics, R, and geographic information systems (GIS)
Wildlife law, policy, and agency process

variations.label: Degree names differ, requirements do not
variations.description: Programs appear as Wildlife Ecology and Management, Wildlife Ecology, Wildlife Biology, or Wildlife and Fisheries. What matters is whether the coursework meets The Wildlife Society (TWS) certification requirements, which many programs are explicitly designed around. TWS has also moved away from requiring a wildlife-titled degree, focusing on the courses taken instead.
variations.source: The Wildlife Society (TWS): wildlife biologist certification

variations.label: Fisheries alongside wildlife
variations.description: Many departments combine wildlife and fisheries, and some curricula let students meet either The Wildlife Society or American Fisheries Society requirements.
variations.source: UMaine: Wildlife, Fisheries, and Conservation Biology

variations.label: From evidence to management
variations.description: Population estimates and habitat analyses feed into species plans, land-management actions, harvest or protection rules, environmental review, permits, and measures of whether an intervention worked.

variations.label: Certification levels
variations.description: TWS offers an associate-level certification for those meeting education requirements and a full certification once experience requirements are met, renewable on a five-year cycle.
variations.source: The Wildlife Society (TWS): wildlife biologist certification

realities: Certification is coursework-driven, which means the specific classes taken as an undergraduate matter more here than almost anywhere else — and that is something you can plan for now.
Entry usually runs through seasonal technician work, often several seasons in different states.
Writing, permitting, and public meetings are part of the job, not a distraction from it.
Agency hiring follows budget cycles and can be slow or intermittent.
